Commentary.Commentary: We are back with the chase. Laura Wolvaardt and Sune Luus have walked out at the top for South Africa Women. Renuka Singh Thakur will be bowling the first over of this chase for India Women.
... The Run Chase ...

The battle for the chase begins - With a target of 186 set, the focus now shifts entirely to how the Indian bowlers exploit the lingering moisture and movement on offer. The game hangs in the balance and will likely be decided by the opening exchange between India’s seamers and the dangerous South African top order. If the Indian bowling unit can maintain their discipline and find early breakthroughs, they could finally secure their first win of the series, otherwise, the Proteas remain favorites to continue their dominant run.

Crucial late partnership bolsters the score - The momentum swung back in India's favor thanks to a resilient sixth-wicket partnership between Richa Ghosh and Deepti Sharma. The pair stitched together a crucial 65-run stand, navigating the tricky conditions to propel the team to the 185-mark. While Jemimah, Deepti, and Richa played the standout hands, the Proteas' bowling unit remained disciplined for the most part, with Eliz-Mari Marx and Kayla Reyneke claiming two wickets each and Tumi Sekhukhune providing support with one.

Middle-order recovery and momentum shifts - The innings did not start ideally for the visitors, who found themselves struggling at 47 for 2 after a stuttering Powerplay. However, Jemimah Rodrigues provided a much-needed spark, accelerating the scoring and anchoring a vital 55-run stand with skipper Harmanpreet Kaur. Just as India seemed to be pulling away, a familiar cluster of wickets in the middle overs threatened to derail the innings, forcing the lower order to absorb immense pressure.

Strategic total in challenging conditions - We have reached the midpoint of the 4th T20I with India Women posting a competitive 185 on the board. While this score is slightly lower than their previous outing, the visitors feel optimistic given that the surface is offering assistance to the bowlers and the subsurface moisture is making stroke-play difficult. On a deck that isn't a traditional flat track, this total represents a significant recovery and a fighting chance to stay alive in the contest.

Commentary.Commentary: We are all set to begin. The two teams stride out in the middle and line up for their respective national anthems. It will be India's national anthem first, followed by that of South Africa. We are now done with the pre-match proceedings. South Africa Women players break from their huddle and spread out, taking up respective field positions. Shafali Verma and Anushka Sharma are the two openers for India Women. Eliz-Mari Marx has the new ball in hand and is raring to go. Let's play...

Pitch Report - Ed Rainsford and Chris Morris describe the Wanderers' surface as a paradise for batters, noting that the hard wicket and thin grass cover are unlikely to dampen the high-scoring nature of the ground. While Rainsford recalls the nearly 400 runs scored here recently, Morris points out that a wet outfield from earlier rain adds a new layer of complexity to the match. Morris emphasizes that bowlers must remain incredibly disciplined, focusing on hitting the top of the off-stump with consistent line and length to create opportunities. Ultimately, both experts anticipate another high-octane contest where the ball will fly and runs will come easily for those who settle in.

South Africa Women (Playing XI) - Laura Wolvaardt (C), Sune Luus, Tazmin Brits, Annerie Dercksen, Kayla Reyneke, Chloe Tryon, Sinalo Jafta (WK), Eliz-Mari Marx (replaces Nadine De Klerk), Ayabonga Khaka (replaces Ayanda Hlubi), Tumi Sekhukhune, Nonkululeko Mlaba.

India Women (Playing XI) - Shafali Verma, Anushka Sharma (replaces Smriti Mandhana), Jemimah Rodrigues, Harmanpreet Kaur (C), Richa Ghosh (WK), Bharti Fulmali, Deepti Sharma, Kashvee Gautam, Kranti Gaud (replaces Arundhati Reddy), Sree Charani (replaces Shreyanka Patil), Renuka Singh Thakur.

Skipper of India Women - Harmanpreet Kaur says that they were good with the bat but they failed to perform with the ball in the previous contest. Kaur adds that they don't have any pressure now so they'll play freely and they have learned from the last game. Ends by saying that she loves to bat and says that they have three changes on their side.

Skipper of South Africa Women - Laura Wolvaardt says they will bowl first as it is easy to chase under lights. She adds that this has been an awesome series and they are good to go. She reckons that they will try and give the same performance as they did earlier. Ends by informing that Ayabonga Khaka and Eliz-Mari Marx are replacing Nadine De Klerk and Ayanda Hlubi.

TOSS - Both skippers have made their way out in the middle. Harmanpreet Kaur has walked out for India Women, while Laura Wolvaardt is out to lead South Africa Women. Laura will be giving the coin a flick. 'Tails' is the call by Harmanpreet Kaur and it lands as 'Heads'. Laura informs that South Africa Women will be BOWLING FIRST.

The deciding factor at the Bullring - For South Africa, this is a prime opportunity to fine-tune their tactics ahead of the T20 World Cup, while India is fighting a desperate battle to snap their losing streak and restore some confidence. The outcome will likely hinge on the Powerplay, unless India can find a way to remove the prolific Laura Wolvaardt early, they risk being overwhelmed by another massive Proteas total or a clinical chase. Stay tuned for toss and team news.

India’s battle for resurgence - For India Women, the series has been a story of missed opportunities despite individual brilliance. Captain Harmanpreet Kaur and opener Shafali Verma found their touch in the previous match with half-centuries, but the bowling unit has struggled to defend totals or contain the South African batters. Key players like Smriti Mandhana and Deepti Sharma will need to step up significantly to provide the balance required to challenge this rampant South African side. India's focus will be on clinical execution in the death overs and finding a way to break the Proteas' opening stands early.

Dominant SA and the quest for a sweep - South Africa Women have been in sublime form, led by captain Laura Wolvaardt, who enters this contest on the back of a stunning century in the 3rd T20I. Their top order, featuring the aggressive Sune Luus and Tazmin Brits, has consistently outplayed the Indian bowlers. Combined with a disciplined bowling attack featuring the likes of Nonkululeko Mlaba and Ayabonga Khaka, the Proteas are using their home-field advantage to full effect. For them, this match is about maintaining momentum and testing their bench strength as they eye a historic 5-0 victory.

A battle for pride amidst Proteas' dominance - Hello and welcome to another exciting installment of the India Women’s tour of South Africa. As we head into the 4th T20I at the Wanderers Stadium in Johannesburg, the hosts, South Africa Women, have already taken a decisive and unassailable 3-0 lead in the five-match series. Despite a high-scoring effort from the visitors in the last game, where they posted 192 runs, the Proteas showed absolute dominance by chasing it down inside 17 overs. While the series is technically decided, this match remains a vital opportunity for India to salvage pride and for South Africa to push for a complete whitewash.
... MATCHDAY ...

Time for Jo'burg part 2 - In a very queer scheduling for this series, where only three venues are rostered for 5 matches, Durban and Jo'burg are two of those who have been given back-to-back matches. That does take away the load of travelling, and unless the same pitch is used again for successive matches, the chances of the deck slowing down should be ruled out. So after a high-scoring encounter on Wednesday, Saturday evening gets prepares itself for another likely massive aggregate. What happened? Not sure, actually. One team batted really well, registering its best batting performance of the series, only to see the contest being blown away by the Powerplay itself. Of course, not literally, but a thunderstorm in the form of Laura Wolvaardt struck the Indians in the second innings and with 72 on the board after 6 overs, without losing any wicket, the target of 193 already seemed like 30-40 runs short. The visitors could barely recover after that early assault and their shoulders started to droop pretty early itself. Dew factor? What else? 100 percent it was the dew factor which made the bowling and fielding very difficult. But given that the Indians play WPL in almost the same conditions back home, one would have expected them to do better. Maybe, it was just the Wolvaardt factor, but the Indians certainly looked dazed and probably did not even realize when did the series slip away. All good? Certain people might want to pinch themselves or increase the brightness of their screen while reading this, but it is true - This series has been touted as the dress rehearsal for the final of the upcoming Women's World Cup. 'Excuse me?' might have been heard from a couple of kangaroos hopping away. Failure to win a World Cup since 2023 has been enough to rule the Aussies out of favouritism for an ICC event and although that's harsh, that's how the system goes. South Africa have been extremely comfortable handling that tag, at least as far the Eves are concerned. Since 2023, they have featured in three successive World Cup finals and although they have not won any, they look pumped up for changing history in 2026. Getting progressively better - That's how the Protea Women will define themselves. Even though the scorecard says won by 6 wickets in the first T20I, people who watched that game would agree if we say that it was the most competitive match of the series thus far. The Indians fought tooth and nail in defending 157 and honestly, South Africa just about got over the line in the end. The second was more of a clinical display with the batting unit firing as a whole while the third was an annihilation. So batting has definitely improved, while the bowling has been pretty good, because even if you say that the African bowling unit conceded more than 190 in the third game, given the way the run chase unfolded, they had restricted India to about 30-40 runs below par. 'Purplish' Green - Ever seen this colour? It doesn't cost to be imaginative. Well, research says that there is indeed such a colour, but our comparison here is that for a legend. Her national team's jersey colour is green, but she is in a purple patch. Given her nickname, 'Wolfie', let's say she is on a prowl. Here are her numbers - 69 | 69 | 51 | 54 | 115. These are Wolvaardt's scores in her last 5 white-ball matches, extending her form from the New Zealand series Down Under. While her team was unable to come out on top in Kiwiland, the results are finally bearing fruit for the management in this series. Toss too crucial? Take nothing away from South Africa, but one feels that they have been a bit lucky as well. All the three matches in this series have been won by the side chasing and barring the first game, the second innings has just been way too easy for the batting side. Yes, India would admit that they could have been better, but sometimes, you just cannot do much with a bar of soap. That's how wet and slippery the ball had got in the first and third matches. It is a concern, if the matches get influenced by the toss. The Indians would hope that they find themselves on the right side of the coin this time around. Form is temporary, but is it a worry? If numbers don't lie, then this losing streak is not a worry for India. After 21st February, 2026, they have not tasted victory even once in 7 matches. That includes 3 ODIs, 3 T20Is and a Test in between. So being winless for 7 matches is definitely a concern. But let's focus on relativity. What's coming up next? T20 World Cup. Then do the results of ODIs and Tests matter much? Definitely not at this stage. Now, let's focus on India's T20I numbers. Since the start of 2025, they have registered 10 wins in this format, which is the joint most among current Test-playing nations (Australia being the other partner). And if you look since their historic World Cup triumph, the Indians have won 7 out of 11 games, with only South Africa ahead at 8 amongst countries who are kind enough to promote the red-ball format in Women's cricket as well. So yes, those 4 losses coming in a quick span might sound a concern, but there is no necessity for any alarm bell to start ringing. Not the best adaptation? A critic might voice that, as far as Indian batting is concerned. Shafali Verma and Harmanpreet Kaur have been the only two players who have been consistent, doing well in all conditions. The other batters have not quite got to terms in judging the conditions. Mind you, it is not just the pitch. Certain areas are played at a high altitude, Johannesburg, for example and you need to adapt physically as well. Surprisingly, spin has done better for India as compared to pace but the visitors need to find a way to strike with the new ball. Form guide (Last 5 completed T20Is, recent first) - SA - W W W L L | IND - L L L W L. Experimentation time? In all likelihood. Both teams look pretty solidly based in terms of their options for the World Cup and both would know that the conditions in England would be far different from the ones here. Additionally, India are playing a 3-match series in England as well against the Brits after this series, so they would focus a bit more on World Cup preparation in that series. They would still want to focus on getting back to winning ways, but these remaining two matches might be more about giving others a chance. South Africa have just two more international matches before their World Cup campaign and they would be eager to carry on their winning momentum. Because they have lesser matches to experiment on, they might want to play with their best possible playing XI for the World Cup. That might suggest a Protean win but count the Indians out at your own risk.
